The headline empirical results are strong: FragFM attains 99.8% validity and 0.58 FCD on MOSES, the best reported GuacaMol FCD score among the compared generators, and substantial improvements in FCD and natural-product-specific distribution metrics on NPGen.

The low-step experiments provide concrete evidence of useful sampling behavior: at 10 steps FragFM retains 96.8% validity and 0.92 FCD, while the atom-level denoising baselines degrade severely. Runtime measurements also suggest a meaningful practical advantage.

Conditional-generation curves consistently favor FragFM over DiGress across basic properties and docking-score surrogates, while preserving high validity. Fragment-bag reweighting is an interesting additional control mechanism.

NPGen targets a relevant and less saturated chemical regime, and the manuscript provides dataset statistics, domain-specific metrics, multiple baseline families, three-run NPGen results, and extensive molecular visualizations.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks ablations for nearly every central design choice: stochastic bags versus a full or fixed vocabulary, bag size, fragment-level versus atom-level flow under a controlled architecture, the latent flow and autoencoder, BRICS fragmentation, auxiliary descriptors/RRWP, and detailed-balance noise. Consequently, the improvements cannot be attributed to the novel fragment-bag mechanism rather than simply using strong fragment priors.

There are substantive mathematical inconsistencies. Equation 40 assigns symmetric mask-to-fragment rates, which do not satisfy the stated detailed-balance equation under the masked marginal p_t(x_1)=t and p_t(M)=1-t except at t=0.5. Equation 33 uses a positive gradient of squared prediction error, whereas a Gaussian log-likelihood produces the negative gradient for the reported positive guidance strengths. Bag construction is also described inconsistently as i.i.d. sampling and sampling without replacement, without specifying how the product-weighted subset distribution in Equation 34 is implemented.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential quantities such as vocabulary sizes, bag size N, latent dimension and variance, graph-size sampling, model widths/depths, batch sizes, training schedule, parameter counts, conditional-regressor training, and random seeds are absent, and no implementation is provided. These omissions also prevent assessing the claimed scaling behavior.

The repeated claim of lossless reconstruction is contradicted by the reported test graph accuracies of 99.93%, 99.42%, and 97.43%. Moreover, the Blossom objective as written does not enforce exactly one connection per coarse edge, maximum cardinality, bond type, or valence constraints; with log-probability weights, the unconstrained matching can even prefer an incomplete matching. Reconstruction errors and their effect on final metrics are not analyzed.

Several comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. NPGen baselines receive uneven tuning, recent fragment-based or molecular-language-model alternatives are absent, and conditional generation is compared only with DiGress. Runtime numbers partly use different hardware, while training cost, memory, preprocessing, and fragment-embedding cost are omitted. Conditional plots provide no sample counts, uncertainty, or diversity/synthesizability results.

The test-fragment experiment is transductive access to test-set building blocks, not evidence that the model autonomously generalizes to unseen fragments; its large scaffold improvement should not support standard benchmark claims. On the ordinary MOSES setting, FragFM also has substantially lower novelty (87.1%) and weaker scaffold similarity than most one-shot baselines, tempering the claim of uniformly superior generation.

NPGen itself needs stronger validation. The stated 85:5:15 split sums to 105% and the reported counts instead imply approximately 80:5:15. A random molecule split risks close-analogue and scaffold leakage in COCONUT; deduplication is not documented. KL direction, smoothing, and continuous-score binning are unspecified, and the learned NPClassifier/NP-likeness surrogates do not establish biological relevance, stereochemical correctness, stability, or synthesizability. No limitations or dual-use discussion accompanies the drug-discovery claims.

Important implementation details contradict one another. Eq. 25 assigns weight 5 to the edge loss and 1 to the node loss, whereas Table 14 reports edge weight 1 and fragment-type weight 5. The ablations do not isolate the sources of improvement. The claimed unseen-fragment generalization experiment supplies fragments extracted directly from the test set. NPGen needs stronger benchmark validation. The paper reports a random molecular split without documenting canonical deduplication, near-duplicate/scaffold overlap, source leakage, or stereochemistry handling, despite stereochemical complexity being central to natural products. NPGen comparisons include only one modern one-shot atom-level model, and the qualitative chemical-plausibility discussion is not backed by quantitative strain, synthesis, or expert evaluation.

The efficiency claim is incomplete: only sampling time is reported, DeFoG uses different hardware, and training cost, autoencoder pretraining cost, peak memory, batch throughput, and parameter-matched comparisons are absent. Several conclusions overstate the evidence: reconstruction is called lossless although NPGen test graph accuracy is 97.43%; conditional generation is compared only with DiGress and docking is assessed solely through the same Smina-based objective; and no code or NPGen release statement is provided. The stochastic-bag formulation is internally inconsistent and insufficiently validated. weaknesses: The stochastic-bag justification has an important inconsistency: the main text assumes i.i.d. marginal samples, whereas the appendix specifies weighted sampling without replacement. The claim of avoiding fixed fragment libraries is overstated. Generation still requires a supplied finite vocabulary and cannot create a genuinely new fragment type. The principal unseen-fragment experiment supplies exact test-set fragments, making it transductive and test-informed rather than evidence of open-world generalization.

NPGen uses a random i.i.d. split and provides no scaffold-split, near-duplicate, or contamination analysis. It also omits stereochemistry and 3D structure despite their central importance for natural products. NPClassifier, NP-likeness, FCD, and RDKit validity do not by themselves establish biological relevance or realistic chemistry.

Claims of overall superiority need qualification: SAFE-GPT substantially outperforms FragFM on every NPGen distributional metric, albeit with lower novelty.
